beginner: Plant acorn squash in rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost mixed in. It is a large, long-season plant, so give it a generous, fertile bed. Many gardeners plant on low hills or mounds, which warm up faster and drain better. If your soil is heavy or stays wet, build up mounds or use raised beds so the roots and developing fruit do not sit in water.
seasoned: Acorn squash wants deep, fertile, well-drained loam rich in organic matter, with steady moisture but no waterlogging. It is a big, long-season vine with hungry roots, so work several inches of compost or rotted manure into the bed before planting. Many growers set plants in low hills or mounds, which warm faster in spring, improve drainage, and give the sprawling vines a clear starting point. Sandy loams warm early and suit the earliest sowings, while heavy clay holds water and invites crown and fruit rot, so amend it generously or build raised mounds.

beginner: Acorn squash likes soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and most garden soil is already close. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand and whether you need to adjust it before planting.
seasoned: Acorn squash does best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.8, with a sweet spot near 6.0 to 6.5. It still grows across a wider band, roughly 5.8 to 7.5, but uptake of some nutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline. Test before planting and lime or add sulfur only on the test's advice rather than by guess.

beginner: Acorn squash grows for a long time and likes steady feeding. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a little extra nitrogen about three to four weeks later as the vines start to run, and again when flowers appear. Once the squash begin to form, go easy on the nitrogen, because too much makes leafy vines instead of fruit.
seasoned: Acorn squash is a moderate feeder over a long season. Work a complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting, then side-dress with nitrogen about three to four weeks after planting as the vines begin to run, and again as flowering starts. Ease off heavy nitrogen once fruit has set, since late, lush vine growth comes at the expense of fruit and draws pests. Pair feeding with even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.

beginner: Your acorn squash vines are spreading. Give them a feeding of nitrogen now.
seasoned: Your acorn squash vines are running, time to side-dress with nitrogen. Keep feeding moderate once fruit sets so the plant builds squash, not just leaves.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a little nitrogen as the vines spread. Do not overdo the nitrogen once fruit forms.
seasoned: A complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress while vines run, easing off once fruit sets. Avoid pushing high nitrogen late, which gives vine at the expense of fruit.

beginner: Mix a balanced fertilizer or a few inches of compost into the soil before planting. Then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer about three to four weeks later, scratched into the soil a few inches away from the plants, and once more when flowers appear.
seasoned: A common rate is a complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked into the bed before planting (roughly 1.5 pounds per 100 square feet, or a balanced scoop per hill), then a nitrogen side-dress about three to four weeks after planting placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeated lightly at flowering.

beginner: The most useful acorn squash companions are flowers that bring in bees, since acorn squash needs lots of bee visits to set fruit, and the traditional Three Sisters partners, corn and beans. Nasturtiums can lure pests away. The one rule that really matters is to keep acorn squash away from other squash, cucumbers, and melons, which all share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Most acorn squash companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on serve two practical ends: pollination and pest pressure. Because cucurbit fruit set is pollinator-limited, with each female flower needing many bee visits, flowering insectary plants like borage near the patch are a genuine help. The Three Sisters partners, corn and beans, give the sprawling vines structure and a nitrogen boost while sharing none of acorn squash's pests, and a trap planting of nasturtium can divert squash bugs and beetles. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep acorn squash away from other cucurbits, which share the full squash pest and disease complex, including the squash vine borer this pepo squash is prone to.

beginner: Corn and acorn squash are the traditional Three Sisters pairing. The corn stands tall while the squash vines spread along the ground, and the big leaves shade out weeds. It is a time-tested combination more than a proven boost.
seasoned: The classic Three Sisters partner: tall corn gives sprawling acorn squash vines structure and light shade in high heat, while the broad squash leaves shade the soil and suppress weeds beneath the corn. A long-standing intercropping tradition with a sound space-and-shade rationale, not a measured yield effect for this exact pair.

beginner: Beans are the third Three Sisters plant. They pull nitrogen from the air into the soil, which the hungry squash appreciates, and they do not share acorn squash's pests. A good, traditional neighbor.
seasoned: The third of the Three Sisters: pole or bush beans fix nitrogen that benefits the long-feeding acorn squash, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near squash to lure squash bugs and beetles away, and their flowers bring in bees, which acorn squash needs to set fruit. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
seasoned: Often planted near cucurbits as a trap and deterrent for squash bugs and cucumber beetles, and its flowers also draw the bees acorn squash depends on for fruit set. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-acorn squash effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

beginner: Borage flowers are loved by bees, and acorn squash needs lots of bee visits to set fruit, so a few borage plants nearby can help with pollination. Mainly grown to bring in bees.
seasoned: A strong bee magnet whose flowers recruit the pollinators that acorn squash fruit set depends on, since each female flower needs many bee visits to size a fruit. Pollinator-habitat value is well grounded; the specific borage-acorn squash pairing is traditional rather than trial-tested.

beginner: Keep acorn squash away from other squash, cucumbers, and melons. They share most of the same pests and diseases, including the squash vine borer, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
seasoned: Cucumber, melon, summer squash, and other winter squash share acorn squash's pest and disease complex, including squash bug, the squash vine borer that readily attacks this pepo squash, cucumber beetle with the bacterial wilt it spreads, and powdery and downy mildew. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them.

beginner: Some gardeners keep potatoes and squash apart, since both are big, hungry plants and potatoes can bring their own diseases. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucurbits compete heavily and that potatoes can harbor disease and attract pests near squash. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

beginner: Leaves get yellow spots, then brown and wilt, and you find clusters of shield-shaped gray-brown bugs and their bronze eggs on the undersides of leaves near the base of the plant.
seasoned: Leaves develop yellow specks that brown and wilt, and heavily fed vines wilt rapidly and turn brittle, a damage pattern sometimes called anasa wilt. Flat bronze egg clusters appear on leaf undersides along the veins, and gray-brown adults and pale nymphs cluster near the crown and under debris.

beginner: Squash bugs pierce the leaves and stems and suck out the juices, which makes the vines wilt. They breed through the summer and hide in plant debris over winter.
seasoned: The squash bug, a true bug that feeds with piercing-sucking mouthparts on cucurbit foliage and stems, injecting saliva that wilts and browns the vines. Populations build through the season and are hardest to control once nymphs are large; the bugs overwinter as adults in garden debris.

beginner: Pick the bugs off by hand and scrape off the egg clusters under the leaves. A board laid on the ground overnight draws them underneath, then lift it in the morning and destroy them. Treat the young bugs with insecticidal soap.
seasoned: Hand-pick adults, crush the egg masses on leaf undersides, and trap bugs by laying a board near the plants overnight, then lifting it in the morning and destroying the cluster underneath. Target young nymphs with insecticidal soap, since large nymphs and adults are tough to kill.

beginner: Cover young plants until they flower, check under the leaves for eggs early in the season, and clean up old vines after harvest so the bugs have nowhere to overwinter.
seasoned: Use row cover on young plants until flowering, clean up vines and debris at season's end to cut overwintering sites, and rotate cucurbits. Scout leaf undersides for the bronze egg clusters from early in the season and act before nymphs mature.

beginner: Small yellow beetles with stripes or spots chew on the leaves and flowers, especially of young plants. Worse, they can spread a disease called bacterial wilt that makes the vines collapse later.
seasoned: Small yellow beetles, striped or spotted, chew young leaves, stems, and flowers, and can scar developing fruit. The bigger threat is indirect: striped and spotted cucumber beetles transmit bacterial wilt, so beetle feeding on seedlings can be followed weeks later by sudden vine wilt.

beginner: Cucumber beetles feed on acorn squash plants and carry the germ that causes bacterial wilt, infecting the plant as they chew. Young seedlings are most at risk.
seasoned: Striped and spotted cucumber beetles feed on cucurbits and carry the bacterium that causes bacterial wilt in their gut, infecting plants as they feed. Seedlings are most vulnerable; once plants have several leaves they tolerate some feeding, and bacterial wilt is generally less severe in winter squash like acorn squash than in cucumber and melon.

beginner: Cover young plants with row cover (remove it when flowers open), pick the beetles off, and use yellow sticky traps. Keeping the beetles down is the best way to avoid the wilt disease they spread.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover removed at flowering, hand-pick beetles, and use yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce numbers. Where bacterial wilt is a known problem, controlling the beetles is the most effective control of the disease, since there is no cure once a plant is infected.

beginner: Cover seedlings until they flower, keep them growing strong, clear away weeds and old plants, and do not plant where squash-family crops grew last year.
seasoned: Exclude beetles from seedlings with row cover, keep young plants vigorous so they grow past the vulnerable stage, clear weeds and debris, and rotate away from where cucurbits grew. Aim control at the early-season colonizers that vector wilt.

beginner: A healthy plant wilts all at once in summer, with what looks like wet sawdust at a hole near the base of the stem and a fat white grub inside. Acorn squash is one of the squashes borers love, so watch for this.
seasoned: A vigorous vine wilts suddenly in mid to late summer, often one runner at a time, with sawdust-like frass oozing from a small hole low on the stem and a fat white caterpillar tunneling inside. As a Cucurbita pepo, acorn squash is a preferred, susceptible host, so a healthy plant can collapse within days once a borer is inside.

beginner: A moth lays eggs at the base of the stem in early summer, and the grubs tunnel inside and kill the vine. The moth likes thin-stemmed squash such as acorn squash and zucchini, so this squash is a common target.
seasoned: The larva of the squash vine borer moth, which lays eggs at the stem base in early summer; the hatching larvae bore into the stem and cut off the plant's water. The moth strongly prefers thin-stemmed Cucurbita pepo squash, which includes acorn squash along with zucchini, spaghetti squash, and summer squash, so this is a pest to plan for rather than hope to avoid.

beginner: Check the base of the stems often in summer. If you find a borer, slit the stem with a knife, dig out the grub, and cover the spot with damp soil so the vine can re-root. Pull and destroy badly damaged vines so the pest does not come back next year.
seasoned: Catch it early: scout the stem base for frass from early summer. If a borer has entered, slit the stem lengthwise with a knife, remove the larva, and mound moist soil over that node to encourage re-rooting. Burying vine joints as they run so a damaged plant can survive on secondary roots, and removing and destroying infested vines at season's end, both reduce next year's brood.

beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they flower, then take it off so bees can reach the blooms. Check the base of the stems for the sawdust-like frass starting in early summer, and clean up old vines after harvest so borers cannot overwinter.
seasoned: Row cover from planting until flowering excludes the egg-laying moths and is the most reliable defense; remove it at bloom so bees can pollinate. Time a planting to dodge the main moth flight where its timing is known, wrap or mound soil over the lower stem, and choose bush or semi-bush types, which some growers find recover better. Scout the stem base for frass from early summer and act at the first sign.

beginner: Tiny soft insects gather on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, making leaves curl and turn yellow, often with a sticky film. They can also spread viruses.
seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often melon aphids, cluster on leaf undersides and growing tips, causing leaves to curl, pucker, and yellow, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. Beyond direct feeding, aphids transmit mosaic viruses that mottle and distort the foliage.

beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck the plant's juices and multiply fast, especially on soft, over-fed growth. The sticky honeydew they leave behind grows black mold.
seasoned: Melon and other aphids suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up quickly on stressed or over-fertilized plants. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold, and several aphid species spread cucurbit mosaic viruses.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control.

beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work instead of spraying everything.
seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants.

beginner: A white, powdery coating spreads over the leaves until they turn yellow and brown and die. The plant fades early, and the squash may not size up or sweeten well.
seasoned: White, powdery patches appear first on the upper and lower leaf surfaces and stems, spreading until leaves yellow, brown, and die back ahead of schedule. Early defoliation cuts the season short, reduces fruit size and the sugars that make acorn squash sweet, and exposes fruit to sunscald.

beginner: A fungus that spreads on warm, humid days, especially where plants are crowded and air does not move well. It does not need wet leaves to take hold.
seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi that thrive in warm conditions with high humidity but do not need leaf wetness, spreading by wind-blown spores. Crowded plantings, poor airflow, and shade worsen it, and it is one of the most common late-season winter-squash diseases.

beginner: Treat early, at the first white spots, with a labeled fungicide like sulfur or horticultural oil, and remove badly affected leaves. Water the soil, not the leaves. Once it covers the plant it is hard to stop.
seasoned: Treat at the first spots, before it spreads, with a labeled fungicide such as sulfur or a horticultural oil or biofungicide, covering both leaf surfaces, and remove the worst leaves. Avoid overhead watering. Once it is widespread, control is mostly damage limitation.

beginner: Pick mildew-tolerant varieties if you can, give plants plenty of room so air moves between them, plant in full sun, and water at the base. Start checking in midsummer and act at the first white spots.
seasoned: Choose mildew-tolerant varieties where available (some acorn squash types such as Honey Bear hold up better), space plants generously for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering. Scout from midsummer and treat at the first sign, since prevention and early action beat rescue.

beginner: Yellow patches show on top of the leaves with fuzzy gray growth underneath, mostly in damp, humid weather. The spots brown and spread until the leaves die.
seasoned: Angular yellow blotches, bounded by the leaf veins, appear on the upper leaf surface, with a grayish or purplish fuzzy growth on the underside in humid weather. Spots brown and coalesce, and severe infection rapidly defoliates the vines.

beginner: A mold-like disease that spreads in wet, humid weather and needs wet leaves to infect. It can move through a planting quickly.
seasoned: A fungus-like water mold that spreads on wind-borne spores and needs leaf wetness and humidity to infect, so it flares in wet, humid spells and dewy conditions. It moves fast once established and is favored by crowding and prolonged leaf wetness.

beginner: Open up the planting so leaves dry faster, remove the worst leaves, and use a labeled fungicide when wet weather sets in. Do not water over the leaves.
seasoned: Improve airflow, let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a labeled fungicide, covering leaf undersides, when conditions favor the disease. Avoid overhead irrigation, which keeps leaves wet and feeds the infection.

beginner: Give plants room so air moves between them, water at the base, and watch closely in humid weather. Choose resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the soil line rather than overhead, choose resistant varieties where available, and avoid working among wet vines. Scout closely in humid weather, when the disease can appear and spread quickly.

beginner: Vines wilt and die even though the soil is wet. If you cut a wilted stem and pull the two ends apart slowly, infected sap stretches into sticky white strings.
seasoned: Individual leaves, then whole vines, wilt and collapse even though the soil is moist, often spreading until the plant dies. A field test helps confirm it: cut a wilted stem and slowly draw the cut ends apart, and infected sap pulls into thin, sticky white strands.

beginner: A germ spread by cucumber beetles as they feed. It blocks the plant's water pipes, so the vine wilts even when watered. Acorn squash is somewhat less prone than cucumbers or melons.
seasoned: A bacterium spread by striped and spotted cucumber beetles, which carry it in their gut and infect plants as they feed. It clogs the water-conducting tissue, so the plant wilts despite adequate water. Winter squash like acorn squash are generally less susceptible than cucumber and melon, but losses still occur.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real fix is keeping cucumber beetles down, since they spread it.
seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy wilting plants to limit spread. Control is really beetle control, so management aims at keeping cucumber beetle numbers down, especially early in the season.

beginner: Keep cucumber beetles under control, since they spread the disease. Cover young plants until they flower, and pull any plant that wilts and tests positive.
seasoned: Manage cucumber beetles from seedling stage with row cover removed at flowering, keep young plants vigorous, and remove infected plants promptly. Controlling the beetle vector is the most effective control of the disease.

beginner: Give acorn squash about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day.
seasoned: Aim for at least 1 inch of water per week, leaning to 1.5 inches in heat or sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. The long-season, big-leaved vine transpires heavily through summer.

beginner: About 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week is a good target, more while the plant is flowering and the squash are growing.
seasoned: Around 1 to 1.5 inches per week is the working range, leaning higher during flowering and fruit sizing and through hot, dry spells. Even, deep watering builds well-formed fruit; let it swing dry and you get poor set and small, uneven squash.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, using a soaker hose or watering wand at the base. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent mildew. As the squash ripen and the skin hardens, ease off the water.
seasoned: Water at the base of the plant with drip or a soaker hose, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves invite powdery and downy mildew. Taper watering as the fruit nears maturity and the rind hardens, which firms the rind for storage, and keep ripening fruit off saturated soil.

beginner: If lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or fruit and stems go soft and rotten, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and soft, rotting stems or fruit at the base point to overwatering or poor drainage. Saturated soil invites crown and fruit rot, especially on heavy ground.

beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry, and drought while fruit is forming gives small, poorly filled squash.
seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is normal in heat, but leaves that stay limp and dull signal real drought. Dry spells during fruit sizing show up as small, poorly filled squash and aborted young fruit.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp until the seedlings come up. Acorn squash is sown into warm ground, so do not let the surface dry out over the seeds.
seasoned: Direct-sown into warm soil, acorn squash wants the seedbed kept evenly moist until emergence; do not let the surface crust over the germinating seed.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered as they get going.
seasoned: Grow the young plants on with steady, even moisture as they build their first true leaves and start to root out.

beginner: As the vine spreads, water deeply at the base, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week and more when hot. Keep the leaves dry to prevent mildew, and mulch to hold the moisture steady.
seasoned: As the long-season, big-leaved vine runs, water deeply at the base, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week and more in heat, with drip or a soaker hose to keep the powdery- and downy-mildew-prone foliage dry. Mulch to hold moisture even.

beginner: Keep the water even once flowers open. Even watering now is what gets the fruit to set well.
seasoned: Flowering through fruit set opens the water-critical stretch. Steady moisture drives good set; a dry check now gives poor set and aborted young fruit.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the squash size up. Letting it dry out and then soaking it gives small, lopsided fruit, so keep the water steady.
seasoned: Fruit sizing is the peak water-critical window: steady, deep moisture builds well-formed, well-filled squash, while a dry-to-wet swing gives small, uneven, misshapen fruit. Keep the ripening fruit up off saturated soil.

beginner: As the squash ripen and the skin hardens, ease right off the water. That dry finish is what firms the skin so they store well through winter.
seasoned: Deliberately ease off watering as the fruit nears maturity and the rind hardens: the dry finish firms the rind so the squash cures and stores well. Saturated soil invites crown and fruit rot on heavy ground. Keep the ripening fruit off wet ground.

beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for acorn squash. It keeps the plant hydrated without encouraging leaf disease.
seasoned: Base watering is the most useful habit for acorn squash, because the same plant that wants steady moisture is also mildew-prone. Keep water on the soil, air moving through the leaves, and the ripening fruit up off wet ground.

beginner: Unlike summer squash, you pick acorn squash once, when it is fully ripe. The best sign is the pale spot where the squash sits on the ground: when it turns from cream or yellow to deep orange, the squash is ready. The rind should also be hard enough that you cannot dent it with a thumbnail, and the stem should be dry and woody. Do not just go by the green color, since acorn squash turns dark green long before it is ripe. Cut the squash off the vine with a knife, leaving a short piece of stem. Bring them in before a hard frost. You can eat acorn squash right away, and you should not cure it the way you would a butternut, since curing actually makes it worse.
seasoned: Harvest acorn squash once at full maturity, not young. The reliable ripeness sign is the ground spot, the patch where the fruit rests on the soil, which turns from cream or yellow to a deep orange; the rind should also be hard enough that a thumbnail cannot dent it, dull rather than glossy, and the stem dried and corky. Do not go by the dark green rind alone, since acorn squash colors up weeks before it is ripe. Cut the fruit from the vine with shears or a knife, leaving a 1 to 2 inch handle of stem, and avoid carrying it by the stem. Get the crop in before a hard frost, which damages the rind and shortens storage. Acorn squash is good to eat straight from the vine and, unlike a butternut, should not be cured: the heat and humidity of curing reduce its quality and shorten its already brief storage.

beginner: If you started seedlings indoors, set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they get used to sun and wind. Be gentle with the roots when you plant, since squash do not like having their roots disturbed.
seasoned: Harden off indoor-started acorn squash over 7 to 10 days, easing the plants into direct sun and wind before transplanting. Handle the rootball gently, because cucurbits resent root disturbance and a checked seedling sulks for weeks; use larger cells and set plants out young, before the roots circle the pot.

beginner: The easiest way to grow acorn squash is to sow seeds right where they will grow, once the soil is warm (about 70°F). Plant a few seeds 1 inch deep in each hill and keep the strongest. Start seeds indoors only if your season is short, about three weeks before planting out, and move them outside while they are still small. In cold areas, use transplants and a fast-maturing variety like Table Ace so the fruit ripens before frost.
seasoned: Because cucurbits resent root disturbance, direct sowing once the soil is reliably warm (at least 65°F, ideally 70°F, at 2 inches) is the simplest, most reliable method, and direct-sown plants quickly catch up. Sow several seeds about 1 inch deep per hill and thin to the strongest. Start seeds indoors only to gain two to three weeks in a short season, sowing in large cells and setting plants out before they outgrow the pot. In the coldest zones, transplants and an early-maturing variety such as Table Ace are what make a fall crop possible.

beginner: Plant three or four seeds in each hill, then keep the one or two strongest seedlings once they grow their first real leaves. Cut the extra ones off at the ground instead of pulling them, so you do not hurt the roots of the ones you keep.
seasoned: Sow three to four seeds per hill and thin to the one or two strongest once they have a true leaf or two. Snip the extras off at soil line rather than pulling, so you do not disturb the roots of the keepers. In rows, thin to one plant every 24 to 36 inches.

beginner: Use a good bagged potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in a pot.
seasoned: Use a rich, free-draining peat- or coir-based potting mix, not garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in a container.

beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer at planting. Pots need feeding more often than beds because watering washes nutrients out.
seasoned: Blend in about a third compost plus a slow-release balanced fertilizer at planting. Because frequent watering flushes nutrients, plan to feed a container acorn squash more regularly than one in the ground.

beginner: Pots dry out much faster than garden beds. In summer a potted acorn squash may need water every day. Check daily and water until it drains from the bottom.
seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, and a acorn squash in a pot can need water once or even twice a day in summer heat. Check daily by feeling the top inch of mix, and water until it runs from the drainage holes; even moisture prevents the small, poorly filled fruit that water swings cause.

seasoned: Feed container acorn squash more often than in-ground ones, since steady watering leaches nutrients. After the slow-release charge at planting, add a balanced liquid feed every 2 to 3 weeks, easing off nitrogen once fruit sets.

seasoned: Not applicable. Acorn squash is a frost-tender annual that completes its life in a single season and is killed by the first hard frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Pull spent vines at season's end and start fresh from seed the following year.

beginner: Acorn squash grows well in a container if you choose a bush type like Table King or Honey Bear, since full-size vining kinds are too big for a pot. Use a large container, at least 10 gallons and 12 inches deep, put it in full sun, keep it well watered (pots dry out fast), and feed it regularly. Water the soil, not the leaves, to help avoid mildew.
seasoned: Acorn squash is one of the more container-friendly winter squashes, because true bush and semi-bush varieties are widely available. Choose a compact type (Table King, Honey Bear, or Table Ace) and give it a big pot: at least 10 gallons and 12 inches deep, larger is better. Give it full sun, let any vines trail out over the rim or up a sturdy support, water at the base daily in heat, and feed regularly, since a small soil volume dries and depletes fast. The container figures here follow general container-vegetable guidance; acorn-squash-specific container numbers are modeled.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which acorn squash likes. Keep the reservoir filled, especially in hot weather, and use a big pot.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits a potted acorn squash well, smoothing the moisture swings this thirsty, mildew-prone plant dislikes. Keep the reservoir topped up in heat, still water from below to keep foliage dry, and use a large enough planter that the roots are not constantly waterlogged.

beginner: An acorn squash keeps at room temperature for about a month or two in a cool spot out of the sun, longer than summer squash but much less than a butternut. Keep it off cold, damp floors so the bottom does not rot.

beginner: Do not put a whole acorn squash in the fridge, it is too cold and makes it break down faster. Once it is cut, wrap the pieces and keep them in the fridge for a few days, or freeze them.
seasoned: Whole acorn squash is not refrigerated; cold storage below about 50°F causes chilling injury and faster breakdown. Cut squash and cooked or pureed flesh, however, should be refrigerated and used within a few days, or frozen.

beginner: Acorn squash freezes well once cooked. Halve and roast or steam it, scoop the flesh out of the skin, cool it, and freeze it in portions. It keeps about a year.
seasoned: Acorn squash freezes well as cooked flesh: halve and roast or steam it, scoop the flesh from the rind, mash it or leave it in chunks, cool, and freeze in measured portions. Frozen cooked acorn squash keeps about a year.

beginner: Acorn squash does not keep as long as other winter squash, only about 1 to 2 months, so plan to eat it within a month or two rather than storing it all winter. You can eat it straight from the vine. Do not cure it the way you would a butternut: for acorn squash, curing actually makes it worse and does not help it keep. Just store it somewhere cool but not cold, about 50 to 55°F, with some air movement, and check it often, since it softens sooner than long-keeping squash.
seasoned: Acorn squash is the shortest keeper of the common winter squashes, storing only about 1 to 2 months, well short of a spaghetti squash and far short of a butternut's 4 to 6. Because it is a Cucurbita pepo, it is fully edible right off the vine and needs no curing. In fact, unlike other winter squash, acorn squash should not be cured at all: the high heat and humidity of a cure reduce its quality, shorten its already brief storage, and can leave the flesh dry and stringy. Instead, once harvested, store it directly, cool but not cold, ideally 50 to 55°F with 50 to 70 percent humidity and good airflow. Store only blemish-free fruit with the stem intact, and check often, since acorn squash softens faster than the long-keeping squashes; eat it within a month or two rather than saving it for late winter.

seasoned: Acorn squash is not a succession crop. It is a single, warm-season planting that sets fruit through summer and matures together for one fall harvest, so you sow once per season rather than at intervals. In most zones a second sowing would be killed by frost before its 80 to 100 day crop could ripen. Only in the warmest, frost-free or near-frost-free zones, or the low desert where a summer sowing is the fall crop, is a second seasonal window viable, and that is a separate season, not a succession.

beginner: Each acorn squash plant has both male and female flowers, so you only need one plant to get fruit. seasoned: Acorn squash is monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a single plant sets fruit with no second variety needed. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and pollen must move from the male to the female blooms. Acorn squash is strongly pollinator-dependent: each female flower needs several bee visits to set a full fruit, and poor pollination shows up as young fruit that yellow and rot at the blossom end, or as small, misshapen squash. Early-season male flowers often open and drop for a week or more before the first females appear, which is normal. Plant flowers nearby, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate with a male flower or small brush in the morning if set stalls.

beginner: Acorn squash is a warm-season squash grown for small, ribbed, heart-shaped fruit with sweet flesh that is perfect halved and roasted. The main things to know: give it a warm season of about 80 to 100 days, water steadily while the fruit grows, watch for squash bugs, squash vine borers, beetles, and mildew, and pick when the skin is hard and dull and the underside spot has turned orange, before frost. seasoned: Acorn squash is a warm-season winter squash (Cucurbita pepo, the same species as zucchini and spaghetti squash) grown for its small, hard-rind, deeply ribbed, heart-shaped fruit with sweet, fine-grained flesh, ideal halved and roasted by the single serving. Unlike its summer-squash cousin zucchini, it is harvested once, at full maturity in fall, when the rind is hard and the pale ground spot where the fruit rests on the soil has turned deep orange. It is the shortest keeper of the common winter squashes, storing only about 1 to 2 months, and, unlike a butternut, it is not cured: curing at high heat actually reduces its quality. Acorn squash comes in both true bush and vining forms, so it suits small gardens as readily as large ones, with vining types running roughly 4 to 8 feet and compact bush types like Table King and Honey Bear staying tidy. It is monoecious, carrying separate male and female flowers on one plant, and fruit set is strongly pollinator-dependent. As a pepo, it is susceptible to the squash vine borer, so managing that pest is part of growing it. The season's shape is set by three things: a warm runway of 80 to 100 frost-free days to mature the crop, moderate pest and disease pressure (squash bug, squash vine borer, cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it spreads, plus powdery and downy mildew), and the single fall harvest, timed at a hard rind with an orange ground spot, before frost.

beginner: Pick a sunny spot with rich, well-drained soil and mix in plenty of compost before planting, since acorn squash is a hungry plant. If your soil is heavy or wet, build the mounds up higher so water drains away from the roots and fruit.
seasoned: Prepare a fertile, well-drained bed in full sun, working several inches of compost or rotted manure into the soil before planting, since acorn squash is a hungry, warm-season plant. Many growers set plants in low hills or mounds about a foot across, which warm faster in spring, drain better, and give the plants a clear starting point. Space to the type: bush and semi-bush acorn squash can go about 18 to 24 inches apart, while vining types want 24 to 36 inches in the row with 3 to 6 feet between rows, since the vines run 4 to 8 feet. On heavy or wet ground, build the mounds up for drainage to head off crown and fruit rot.

seasoned: Acorn squash is the most forgiving winter squash for the maritime Pacific Northwest's cool, marine-tempered summer: at 80 to 100 days to maturity it is short enough to size up and cure before the wet fall closes in. Start seeds indoors in early April for a jump on the season, then set out in May once the soil is reliably warm; direct sowing in May also works once soil temperature allows. Vines size up through June and July, and the crop ripens from mid to late summer into October. Favor a fast, often bush-habit variety such as Table Ace, especially in the cooler, foggier coastal pockets, and cure fruit a week or two in a warm, dry spot before storage, since the region's autumn rain can undercut curing on the vine (OSU / WSU).
